scope: AQA Physics 7408 AS electricity and Chemistry 7405 AS RP4 observations, Group 2 and Group 7; mock-only; no untaught topics.
notes: Eight newly authored paper-style reasoning problems. Chemical prompts are interpretation of stated theoretical observations, not instructions for conducting tests; no operational laboratory method. Auto suggested marks are provisional, correct alternative methods need human review. Not copied past paper questions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style evidence and data practice
questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: NTC thermistor in upper potential divider branch
questions.prompt: An ideal 12.0 V source powers a potential divider. The upper component is an NTC thermistor; the lower component is a fixed 3.00 kΩ resistor, and output Vout is measured across the lower resistor. When cool, the thermistor is 6.00 kΩ; when warm, it is 2.00 kΩ. No load is attached. (a) Calculate the total resistance, current and Vout for the cool condition. (b) Recalculate the total resistance, current and Vout when warm. (c) Explain the voltage change without assuming a thermistor has constant resistance. [7 marks]
markPoints: Initially the series total resistance is 6.00 + 3.00 = 9.00 kΩ.
Initial current is 12.0 V/9000 Ω = 1.33 mA.
Initial output across the lower fixed resistor is Vout=12.0×3/(6+3)=4.00 V.
After warming the total series resistance becomes 2.00+3.00=5.00 kΩ.
Warm current is I=12.0/5000=2.40 mA.
Warm output voltage is Vout=12.0×3/(2+3)=7.20 V.
NTC resistance falls as temperature rises, so more of the supply p.d. is across the unchanged lower resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: Initially the series total resistance is 6.00 + 3.00 = 9.00 kΩ. Initial current is 12.0 V/9000 Ω = 1.33 mA. Initial output across the lower fixed resistor is Vout=12.0×3/(6+3)=4.00 V. After warming the total series resistance becomes 2.00+3.00=5.00 kΩ. Warm current is I=12.0/5000=2.40 mA. Warm output voltage is Vout=12.0×3/(2+3)=7.20 V. NTC resistance falls as temperature rises, so more of the supply p.d. is across the unchanged lower resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style evidence and data practice
questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Identical cells in series and parallel with internal resistance
questions.prompt: Two identical cells each have emf 1.50 V and internal resistance 0.300 Ω. A 2.40 Ω resistor is connected as the external load. In arrangement S the two cells are in series; in arrangement P they are in parallel with the same polarity. Assume identical cells and ideal connecting wires. (a) Calculate combined emf and internal resistance for S, then load current and terminal p.d. (b) Repeat for P. (c) Explain why the two arrangements produce different currents. [8 marks]
markPoints: In series the combined emf is εS=1.50+1.50=3.00 V.
In series the internal resistances add, giving rS=0.300+0.300=0.600 Ω.
Series load current IS=3.00/(2.40+0.600)=1.00 A.
Series terminal p.d. across load VS=1.00×2.40=2.40 V.
For identical cells in parallel the combined emf is εP=1.50 V, unchanged.
Parallel internal resistance is rP=0.300/2=0.150 Ω.
Parallel load current IP=1.50/(2.40+0.150)=0.588 A and terminal p.d. VP≈1.41 V.
The series arrangement has larger combined emf, whereas parallel reduces internal resistance without increasing emf; the resulting load currents differ.
questions.modelAnswer: In series the combined emf is εS=1.50+1.50=3.00 V. In series the internal resistances add, giving rS=0.300+0.300=0.600 Ω. Series load current IS=3.00/(2.40+0.600)=1.00 A. Series terminal p.d. across load VS=1.00×2.40=2.40 V. For identical cells in parallel the combined emf is εP=1.50 V, unchanged. Parallel internal resistance is rP=0.300/2=0.150 Ω. Parallel load current IP=1.50/(2.40+0.150)=0.588 A and terminal p.d. VP≈1.41 V. The series arrangement has larger combined emf, whereas parallel reduces internal resistance without increasing emf; the resulting load currents differ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style evidence and data practice
questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Filament lamp non-ohmic behaviour from numerical I–V data
questions.prompt: An idealised filament lamp has the following simultaneous readings: at V=1.00 V, I=0.200 A; at V=3.00 V, I=0.400 A; at V=6.00 V, I=0.600 A. (a) Calculate resistance R=V/I at each reading. (b) Decide whether this is consistent with a constant-resistance conductor and justify using the values. (c) Explain the physical reason for the resistance change. (d) Distinguish resistance V/I at one operating point from the local gradient of a current-against-voltage graph. [7 marks]
markPoints: Resistance rises as voltage and current increase, so the lamp is not ohmic under changing conditions.
Greater current heats the filament to a higher temperature.
In the hotter metal lattice, electron collisions are more frequent, increasing resistance.
R=V/I is the operating-point ratio; the local gradient dI/dV on an I–V curve is differential conductance, not generally 1/(V/I) for a curved graph.
questions.modelAnswer: At 1.00 V, R=1.00/0.200=5.00 Ω. At 3.00 V, R=3.00/0.400=7.50 Ω. At 6.00 V, R=6.00/0.600=10.0 Ω. Resistance rises as voltage and current increase, so the lamp is not ohmic under changing conditions. Greater current heats the filament to a higher temperature. In the hotter metal lattice, electron collisions are more frequent, increasing resistance. R=V/I is the operating-point ratio; the local gradient dI/dV on an I–V curve is differential conductance, not generally 1/(V/I) for a curved graph.

questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Loaded resistor divider: parallel equivalent and current change
questions.prompt: A 9.00 V ideal source feeds a potential divider consisting of an upper 3.00 kΩ resistor and lower 6.00 kΩ resistor. The output is taken across the lower resistor. An additional 6.00 kΩ load is then connected in parallel across the output. (a) Find the unloaded Vout and source current. (b) Find the effective lower resistance after loading, new Vout and source current. (c) State the direction of change in both voltage and supply current and explain. [7 marks]
markPoints: Unloaded resistance is 3.00+6.00=9.00 kΩ.
Unloaded source current is 9.00 V/9000 Ω = 1.00 mA.
Unloaded output Vout=9.00×6/(3+6)=6.00 V.
Adding 6.00 kΩ in parallel with 6.00 kΩ gives lower equivalent R=3.00 kΩ.
Loaded total resistance is 3.00+3.00=6.00 kΩ.
Loaded output Vout=9.00×3/(3+3)=4.50 V and source current 9.00/6000=1.50 mA.
Loading reduces lower resistance, so output falls from 6.00 to 4.50 V while source current rises from 1.00 to 1.50 mA.
questions.modelAnswer: Unloaded resistance is 3.00+6.00=9.00 kΩ. Unloaded source current is 9.00 V/9000 Ω = 1.00 mA. Unloaded output Vout=9.00×6/(3+6)=6.00 V. Adding 6.00 kΩ in parallel with 6.00 kΩ gives lower equivalent R=3.00 kΩ. Loaded total resistance is 3.00+3.00=6.00 kΩ. Loaded output Vout=9.00×3/(3+3)=4.50 V and source current 9.00/6000=1.50 mA. Loading reduces lower resistance, so output falls from 6.00 to 4.50 V while source current rises from 1.00 to 1.50 mA.

questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Identify mixed halides using silver-halide observations
questions.prompt: An imagined sample contains two different halide ions. After a diagnostic precipitation reaction the solid appears white and cream in separate portions. On exposure to dilute aqueous ammonia the white portion disappears while the cream remains; with concentrated aqueous ammonia the remaining cream portion dissolves. (a) Identify the two halide ions and name both silver-halide precipitates. (b) Explain what the differing ammonia observations tell you. (c) Give one appropriate net ionic precipitation equation. (d) Explain why an iodide-only interpretation does not fit the complete evidence. [7 marks]
markPoints: The white precipitate is silver chloride, AgCl.
The cream precipitate is silver bromide, AgBr.
Therefore the mixture is consistent with chloride ions Cl⁻ and bromide ions Br⁻.
Silver chloride dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia.
Silver bromide requires concentrated aqueous ammonia for dissolution in this conventional test.
A correct net ionic equation is Ag⁺(aq)+Cl⁻(aq)→AgCl(s) or Ag⁺(aq)+Br⁻(aq)→AgBr(s).
Silver iodide AgI is yellow and remains insoluble even in concentrated aqueous ammonia, so iodide alone cannot explain the observations.
questions.modelAnswer: The white precipitate is silver chloride, AgCl. The cream precipitate is silver bromide, AgBr. Therefore the mixture is consistent with chloride ions Cl⁻ and bromide ions Br⁻. Silver chloride dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia. Silver bromide requires concentrated aqueous ammonia for dissolution in this conventional test. A correct net ionic equation is Ag⁺(aq)+Cl⁻(aq)→AgCl(s) or Ag⁺(aq)+Br⁻(aq)→AgBr(s). Silver iodide AgI is yellow and remains insoluble even in concentrated aqueous ammonia, so iodide alone cannot explain the observations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style evidence and data practice
questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Discriminate sulfate and carbonate precipitation evidence
questions.prompt: Two theoretical aqueous samples A and B give white solids in the presence of Ba²⁺ ions. In a second observation, the solid from A disappears when acidic conditions are present, with gas bubbles; the white solid from B persists in acidic conditions. Explain which common anions are consistent with A and B, use two net ionic precipitation equations and one equation for the gas-producing process, and explain why an unacidified white barium precipitate alone is not a specific sulfate identification. [7 marks]
markPoints: Sample A is consistent with carbonate ions CO₃²⁻ giving barium carbonate.
Sample B is consistent with sulfate ions SO₄²⁻ giving insoluble barium sulfate.
Carbonate precipitation: Ba²⁺(aq)+CO₃²⁻(aq)→BaCO₃(s).
Sulfate precipitation: Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s).
The carbonate solid can disappear under acidic conditions as carbonate reacts with H⁺.
Carbonate and acid give gas: CO₃²⁻+2H⁺→CO₂+H₂O.
Both carbonate and sulfate can form white barium solids in unacidified conditions, hence acidified sulfate testing avoids this carbonate false positive.
questions.modelAnswer: Sample A is consistent with carbonate ions CO₃²⁻ giving barium carbonate. Sample B is consistent with sulfate ions SO₄²⁻ giving insoluble barium sulfate. Carbonate precipitation: Ba²⁺(aq)+CO₃²⁻(aq)→BaCO₃(s). Sulfate precipitation: Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s). The carbonate solid can disappear under acidic conditions as carbonate reacts with H⁺. Carbonate and acid give gas: CO₃²⁻+2H⁺→CO₂+H₂O. Both carbonate and sulfate can form white barium solids in unacidified conditions, hence acidified sulfate testing avoids this carbonate false positive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style evidence and data practice
questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Group 2 solubility trends and specified uses
questions.prompt: For Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates from Mg to Ba, give the direction of each solubility trend in water. Then explain why the stated observations fit those trends: magnesium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble whereas barium sulfate is insoluble. Identify the appropriate uses of Mg(OH)₂ in medicine, Ca(OH)₂ in agriculture, CaO or CaCO₃ in flue-gas treatment, and insoluble BaSO₄ in medicine. [7 marks]
markPoints: Group 2 hydroxide solubility generally increases down the group.
Group 2 sulfate solubility generally decreases down the group.
Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, consistent with the lower end of the increasing hydroxide trend.
Barium sulfate is insoluble, consistent with decreasing sulfate solubility from Mg to Ba.
Magnesium hydroxide acts as an antacid, neutralising excess stomach acid.
Calcium hydroxide raises the pH of acidic agricultural soil; CaO or CaCO₃ can remove acidic SO₂ from flue gases.
BaSO₄ is used as an X-ray contrast agent in medicine because its very low solubility limits absorption of barium ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Group 2 hydroxide solubility generally increases down the group. Group 2 sulfate solubility generally decreases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, consistent with the lower end of the increasing hydroxide trend. Barium sulfate is insoluble, consistent with decreasing sulfate solubility from Mg to Ba. Magnesium hydroxide acts as an antacid, neutralising excess stomach acid. Calcium hydroxide raises the pH of acidic agricultural soil; CaO or CaCO₃ can remove acidic SO₂ from flue gases. BaSO₄ is used as an X-ray contrast agent in medicine because its very low solubility limits absorption of barium ions.

questions.question: Mock applied evidence challenge
questions.subtopic: Halogen displacement and oxidising versus reducing trends
questions.prompt: Consider theoretical aqueous reactions among Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ and the halide ions Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻. (a) Write ionic equations for chlorine displacing bromide and for bromine displacing iodide. (b) Would iodine displace chloride? Explain. (c) State the trend in oxidising ability of the halogens down Group 7 and the opposing trend in reducing ability of their halide ions. (d) Identify the species oxidised and reduced in Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. [7 marks]
markPoints: Chlorine displaces bromide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.
Bromine displaces iodide: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.
Iodine does not displace chloride because iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine.
Halogen oxidising ability decreases down Group 7.
Halide-ion reducing ability increases down Group 7.
In the chlorine/bromide reaction Br⁻ loses electrons to become Br₂ and is oxidised.
Cl₂ gains electrons to become Cl⁻ and is reduced.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine displaces bromide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Bromine displaces iodide: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Iodine does not displace chloride because iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine. Halogen oxidising ability decreases down Group 7. Halide-ion reducing ability increases down Group 7. In the chlorine/bromide reaction Br⁻ loses electrons to become Br₂ and is oxidised. Cl₂ gains electrons to become Cl⁻ and is reduced.
